title: Explain the catfish
intro: Pick one option. Both count as completing the activity.

paths.label: Explain the catfish to a friend
paths.prompt: Imagine a friend has never seen an African catfish. In a few sentences, describe what it looks like and one thing that makes it a good farm fish. Use what you saw in the 3D model and photos.
paths.example: It has a long, eel-like body with smooth skin and no scales, a flat head and four pairs of whiskers called barbels that help it find food. Its back fin runs almost to the tail. It can breathe air, which makes it hardy.

paths.label: Help someone choose fingerlings
paths.prompt: Read Bisi's question. What would you tell her about fingerling sizes, and what should she ask the seller?
paths.scenario: Bisi (fictional) is buying her first catfish fingerlings. At the hatchery she sees one batch where all the fish look about the same small size, and another, cheaper batch with a mix of tiny and much bigger fingerlings together. She asks you which batch makes more sense and why.

modelPoints.point: Mixed sizes are risky because larger fingerlings can eat smaller ones (cannibalism).
In FAO's trials most fingerlings were about 2–3 g and a minority 8–10 g after four to five weeks, so size differences are normal and need managing.
Cheaper isn't better if many fish are lost; she should ask how the batch was graded.
She can ask the seller about the age and size of the fingerlings and whether sizes were sorted.

rubric.description: Describes the long, eel-like body, smooth scaleless skin or flat head.
Mentions the barbels or the long dorsal/anal fins.
Explains that catfish can breathe air, making them hardy.
Shows understanding of fingerlings and why size differences matter.
Connects the fish's traits to practical farming choices.
Names a sensible question to ask or something still to find out.
